opportunities.title: Quote-intake and rate-response agent for drayage, LTL and transload requests
opportunities.problem: Every commercial entry point is unstructured and human-gated. The site says 'call today for a free, no obligation quote' on the drayage, LTL, transloading and cross-dock pages, and the only web form collects name, email and message behind an arithmetic captcha - no lane, weight, commodity, accessorial, appointment-window or piece-count fields. Requests therefore arrive as phone calls and free-text emails that a rep must re-key before pricing, and warehouse value-add work (strip, sort, palletize, wrap) is quoted per job, so each transload request needs bespoke estimating. With 12 drivers, 17 power units and a small shared back office, inbound quoting queues behind phone and dispatch work.
evidence: Site routes all quoting to the phone line ('free, no obligation quote') and publishes only a three-field contact form with a math captcha; no online quote, booking or rate tool exists (https://totalsourcelogistics.com/).
Warehouse value-add work - strip, sort, palletize, wrap, cross-dock - is priced per job, so transloading quotes require manual estimating (https://totalsourcelogistics.com/).

O*NET lists 'estimate freight rates and record shipment costs and weights' and 'prepare bills of lading, invoices and other shipping documents' as core cargo-and-freight-agent tasks - the clerical quoting layer the brief flags as wage-pressured (https://www.onetonline.org/link/summary/43-5011.00).

NJ cargo and freight agents median $28.80/hr, mean $28.54/hr ($59,360/yr mean), 3,340 employed - the benchmark cost of the labor this displaces (https://web.archive.org/web/20250318091039/https://www.bls.gov/oes/current/oes_nj.htm).
Company already runs Portpro intermodal TMS, so a pricing/rules source and a place to write quote records exist (https://totalsourcelogistics.com/).
opportunities.agent_design: Trigger-based intake agent that watches the dispatch@ inbox, the web form and (in a later phase) transcribed voicemails, and normalises each request into a structured shipment: origin/destination, port vs dock vs consignee, container or LTL, weight, pieces, commodity, hazmat flag, appointment window, accessorials. It looks up the lane in the rate table / Portpro, applies accessorial and minimum-charge rules, and drafts a quote email plus a TMS quote record. Pricing formula stays deterministic (a rules table), with the model used only to read the request and write the response - the pattern the freight-negotiation working paper found achieved broker-level results with auditable decisions (https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.20732). Human approval is mandatory for: new lanes with no rate on file, hazmat/chemical cargo (shipping-paper rules under 49 CFR Part 172), anything above a value or discount threshold, and any request the agent cannot fully parse - those route to a rep with a filled-in summary. Records are written to a durable log for later rate-history and dispute use, not left in a chat thread.
opportunities.why_not_DIY: A chatbot subscription cannot read a TMS rate table, apply accessorial and minimum-charge logic, write a quote record back to Portpro, or hold a lane-level approval threshold. It also cannot keep shipper-specific rates confidential - those terms are commercially sensitive and need tenant-isolated retrieval and retention controls rather than a public consumer endpoint. Reliability matters more than fluency here: a wrong price quoted to an importer is a billed loss, so deterministic pricing plus human sign-off on exceptions is the product.

impact_estimate.range: $3,500-$14,000/yr in recovered freight-agent/CSR hours, plus faster turnaround that is not priced here
impact_estimate.assumptions: Inference, not a measured figure: 15-30 inbound quote/rate requests per week (six service lines, 400+ partner units, 800,000 reported miles) at 15-25 minutes of clerical gather-price-write-up each = 195-650 hrs/yr; the agent removes 50-65% of that clerical time = ~100-420 hrs/yr; valued at $28.54/hr mean NJ cargo-and-freight-agent wage plus ~25% payroll burden (~$35/hr). Excludes any win-rate gain from same-hour quotes, which is the larger commercial upside but cannot be evidenced from public data.

opportunities.pilot_scope: 3 weeks against a backfill of the last 60-90 days of quote emails plus live form traffic: a working intake-and-draft service that produces structured quote records and draft replies for one segment (LTL NJ/NYC or port drayage), a rules table seeded from current rate sheets, an exception queue with approval UI, and a scorecard showing median time-to-draft versus the current baseline. No autonomous sending in the pilot.

opportunities.title: Load-status, appointment and exception agent with a working customer portal (replaces the dead 'Client Portal' link)
opportunities.problem: Customers have no self-service path. The main navigation's 'Client Portal' points at https://www.lpagrouponline.net/clientportal, a hostname that does not resolve, and the site publishes no booking, scheduling or tracking login - only one toll-free number, a dispatch email and the promise that management is reachable 24/7. Status therefore arrives by humans answering calls and re-keying Portpro and Verizon GPS data, across two nodes (Avenel LTL dock and the 26,000 sq ft bonded CFS near Port Elizabeth) and a partner fleet of 400+ units. That is the same coordination layer where the literature measures real lost time: detention and gate-queue costs, not driving, are where for-hire carriers leak hours.
evidence: The 'Client Portal' navigation link points to lpagrouponline.net, which does not resolve - the self-service project appears stalled or abandoned (https://totalsourcelogistics.com/).
No live chat, booking widget, scheduling tool or online tracking login exists; contact is one toll-free number plus dispatch@totalsourcelogistics.com (https://totalsourcelogistics.com/).

Site claims management staff are reachable 24/7 and personally oversee routing, dispatching, cubing and loading - after-hours coverage is staff phones, not a system (https://totalsourcelogistics.com/).

USDOT study: drivers are detained past the 2-hour free time on roughly 1 in 10 stops for an average of 1.4 extra hours (3.4 hours total at the facility), with for-hire truckload carriers detained about 5x as often as private carriers (https://doi.org/10.21949/1502646).

An adaptive truck-appointment simulation at a container port cut maximum queue length ~62% with only 7.8% of arrivals rescheduled - appointment coordination, not more dispatchers, is the lever (https://doi.org/10.3390/su17135740).

NJ dispatchers median $24.32/hr, mean $26.64/hr ($55,410/yr mean), 6,390 employed - the cost of the status-call and appointment labor (https://web.archive.org/web/20250318091039/https://www.bls.gov/oes/current/oes_nj.htm).
opportunities.agent_design: Event-driven agent on top of Portpro (load/stop/container status, POD images) and Verizon GPS telemetry. Triggers: container available or discharged, driver geofence arrival/departure at terminal, dock or consignee, appointment window approaching, dwell exceeding a threshold, missing POD or signature. Actions: push proactive status updates to the requesting customer (email first, SMS/portal later) on an exception basis; assemble and confirm terminal and dock appointment slots; flag at-risk loads to the dispatcher; draft the POD-backed invoice trigger once signature capture is confirmed. A rebuilt, working customer portal (replacing the dead link) gives per-customer load visibility, POD download and a structured quote/booking request form feeding opportunity 1. Human approval: every schedule change, any rebooking or detention/accessorial charge, any customer-facing message the model is not confident about, and all hazmat or bonded-CFS paperwork. Agents read and flag HOS/ELD and terminal-portal data; they never author or edit HOS records.
opportunities.why_not_DIY: This is multi-system integration with real-world side effects: a TMS, a telematics feed, third-party terminal appointment portals controlled by the port, plus a customer-facing surface. A chatbot cannot book a terminal slot, notice a truck has sat 90 minutes, or reconcile a POD to a stop. The work also has to survive unattended operation - duplicate updates, stale GPS, partial TMS records - and must keep customer rate and shipment data isolated per account, which consumer LLM products do not offer.

impact_estimate.range: $2,500-$11,000/yr in dispatch/CSR hours; detention and dwell reduction left unquantified (upside only)
impact_estimate.assumptions: Inference: 10-20 inbound status/check calls per day at 3-5 minutes each = 125-415 hrs/yr, 60-80% absorbable = ~75-330 hrs/yr at $26.64/hr mean NJ dispatcher wage plus ~25% burden (~$33/hr). Detention is deliberately excluded from the dollar range because TSL's stop mix, free-time terms and accessorial recovery are unknown; the USDOT study (1 in 10 stops, 1.4 extra hours) sits above the national baseline for for-hire truckload, and the port-appointment simulation suggests queue-length effects of that order are achievable, but neither is a measurement of this carrier.

opportunities.pilot_scope: 4 weeks on one customer cohort and 10-15 daily loads: Portpro + Verizon read integration, a live status feed, a rebuilt client-portal page (login, load list, POD download, quote request form), automated proactive notifications for arrival/departure and at-risk dwell, an exception queue for dispatchers, and a weekly report of calls displaced and dwell versus the pre-pilot baseline. Appointment write-back to terminal portals scoped but may land in phase 2 if portal access is gated.

opportunities.title: Inspection-readiness and defect-triage agent for the 17-unit fleet (vision pre-trip checks + document/HOS signals)
opportunities.problem: FMCSA's 24-month snapshot shows a 33.3% vehicle out-of-service rate against a 22.26% national average - roughly one in three roadside inspections ends with a truck placed out of service, on a fleet with zero reportable crashes and a Satisfactory rating. That gap is an inspection-readiness and preventive-maintenance signal, not a policy gap: defects are being found by the roadside instead of at the dock. Each event pulls a unit out of a 17-unit fleet that logs about 800,000 miles a year, and roadside OOS history is visible to the shippers, brokers and 3PLs that qualify carriers.
evidence: FMCSA SAFER for USDOT 691684: 12 US roadside inspections in the 24 months to 11/09/2026, vehicle out-of-service rate 33.3% versus 22.26% national, 17 power units, 12 drivers, ~800,000 miles for 2025 (https://safer.fmcsa.dot.gov/query.asp?searchtype=ANY&query_type=queryCarrierSnapshot&query_param=USDOT&original_query_param=NAME&query_string=691684&original_query_string=TOTAL%20SOURCE%20LOGISTICS%20INC).

O*NET lists 'maintain logs of working hours and of vehicle service/repair status to satisfy state and federal rules' and 'check all load-related documentation for completeness and accuracy before dispatch/delivery' as core driver tasks - the manual checking loop that fails at the roadside (https://www.onetonline.org/link/summary/53-3032.00).

Working paper (arXiv preprint, not peer-reviewed) constructing abilities-based robotics/AI exposure indices: trucking and warehousing rank among the most exposed industries to physical automation, but the authors state the measure captures technical relatedness, not readiness, cost or adoption - so scope this narrowly and expect edge cases (https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.24267).

NJ heavy/tractor-trailer driver benchmark: $30.04/hr median, $30.90/hr mean ($64,270/yr mean), 52,580 employed - driver time is the expensive input, so a failed inspection that idles a driver is the cost driver (https://web.archive.org/web/20250318091039/https://www.bls.gov/oes/current/oes_nj.htm).
opportunities.agent_design: Edge + document agent on 3-5 units first. Edge: cab-mounted cameras/dash units photograph the tractor/trailer at pre-trip and at yard entry/exit; a vision model checks the specific items that drive common OOS findings (lights/markers, tire condition, conspicuity tape, securement, placards, mud flaps), and anything it cannot verify at >threshold confidence becomes a human or driver check, not a pass. Document/knowledge layer: aggregates DVIRs, repair orders, PM schedules and prior inspection results into a per-unit readiness score, routes defects to a work-order draft with photo evidence, and answers driver/shop questions from the carrier's own maintenance SOPs and FMCSA inspection criteria (capability C inside the same deployment). A separate read-only compliance agent watches ELD/HOS and driver-qualification file expiry and flags gaps to management. Human approval: every repair authorization, every OOS-adjacent judgement, and all safety-sensitive dispositions stay with the maintenance lead or a named manager. Hardware and the private model endpoint sit on-prem/tenant-isolated - no driver camera footage or CDL/medical data on a public consumer LLM.
opportunities.why_not_DIY: Requires cameras and yard/edge inference, not a text subscription; vision accuracy on dirty, night-time, wet-lens conditions has to be measured on this fleet, not assumed. It also needs integration to maintenance records and ELD, per-unit history, and a private deployment because driver images, CDL/medical certificate dates and Clearinghouse status are sensitive personal data that carriers and insurers expect to stay in a controlled environment.

impact_estimate.range: $1,500-$5,000/yr in avoided lost unit-days and re-inspection cost; larger unquantified value in shipper qualification and crash/claim exposure
impact_estimate.assumptions: Inference: 12 inspections over 24 months at a 33.3% vehicle OOS rate implies roughly 4 OOS events in two years (~2/yr). Assume 1-2 revenue days lost per event; revenue per unit-day inferred from 800,000 miles / 17 units / ~250 operating days = ~188 mi/day at an assumed $2.50-$3.00 all-in revenue per mile = $470-$565/unit-day. 2 events x 1.5 days x ~$520 = ~$1,560/yr, plus $200-$400/event in re-inspection and shop rework. Excluded as unpriced upside: reduced roadside repair cost, insurance/claim effect, and broker or shipper scorecard screening that treats OOS history as a disqualifier. Range is intentionally conservative - this is the smallest dollar case of the three even though its evidence is the hardest.

opportunities.pilot_scope: 4 weeks on 3-5 units at the Avenel/Elizabeth yard: camera install and night/day accuracy baseline on the target defect list, a per-unit readiness dashboard fed by DVIR and repair-order data, defect-to-work-order drafts with photo evidence, an HOS/driver-qualification expiry watchlist, and a measured before/after on defects caught in the yard versus at inspection. Explicit go/no-go: only scale past 5 units if yard-caught defects exceed roadside-caught defects in the pilot window.

lead_score.rationale: Pain (22/30): unusually hard, company-specific signals for a small carrier - a dead 'Client Portal' hostname, phone-only quoting with a three-field form, a 33.3% vehicle OOS rate versus 22.26% national, and a 24/7 promise carried by staff phones. Docked because there are zero readable customer reviews, no complaints or owner statements, and everything about volume and internal workflow is inferred from a 2022-vintage website plus FMCSA records. Fit (18/20): three of the four biggest leaks here - intake/quoting, status and appointment coordination, inspection readiness - map directly onto A and E, with Portpro as a real integration anchor rather than a hypothetical one. Ability to pay (12/20): 17 power units and ~800,000 miles/yr imply a low-single-digit-million revenue base, regional carrier margins are thin, and revenue, headcount and customer concentration are all unverified - there is budget for a scoped pilot and a retainer, not a large transformation. Ease (10/15): the buying group is small and the systems are few, but the decision maker is unknown (no leadership page; only a registered agent, Mark Silverstein, in the state filing), the site carries contradictory facility addresses, and Portpro/terminal-portal access will need cooperation that a 3-4 week pilot can be blocked on. Strategic (13/15): port drayage and LTL carriers clustered around Port Newark/Elizabeth and Avenel look nearly identical - bonded CFS, small power fleet, partner overflow capacity, phone-and-email back office - so the quote-intake and status agents and the OOS-readiness scorecard are reusable across dozens of local prospects with only rate-table and TMS-connector changes.

best_evidence_signal: FMCSA shows a 33.3% vehicle out-of-service rate against a 22.26% national average over 24 months on 12 inspections, while the company's own 'Client Portal' link points to a domain that no longer resolves - two measurable operational gaps in one small carrier (https://safer.fmcsa.dot.gov/query.asp?searchtype=ANY&query_type=queryCarrierSnapshot&query_param=USDOT&original_query_param=NAME&query_string=691684&original_query_string=TOTAL%20SOURCE%20LOGISTICS%20INC).
